newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia believes will improve ties with US, EU.
newsitem.headline: Croatia believes will improve ties with US, EU.

text.p: Croatia said on Friday it was taking steps to improve relations with the United States and the European Union after ties deteriorated over Zagreb's alleged lack of commitment to the Balkan peace process.

Washington stepped up pressure in early July when it vetoed a discussion on World Bank's $30 million loan to Croatia, citing insufficient compliance with obligations Zagreb assumed under the 1995 Dayton peace agreement.
The agreement calls for cooperation with a U.N. war crimes tribunal, return of all persons displaced by war and throwing its weight behind Bosnia's fragile Croat-Moslem federation.

"We believe that certain events regarding peaceful reintegration (of the last Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia), an agreeement on joint police (in Bosnia)...and new initiatives related to the cooperation with the International War Crimes Tribunal (ICTY) ... that these firm arguments will make some impact," Foreign Minister Mate Granic told reporters.
He spoke ahead of the visit of U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Bill Richardson, who was due to meet president Franjo Tudjman on Saturday.

"As far as the cooperation with the Tribunal is concerned there have been certain new elements," he said, referring to the fact that the dozen Bosnian Croat suspects recently told the Tribunal they would hand themelves in voluntarily if granted a quick and fair trial.
Tudjman recently told Reuters that Croatia would extradite all Boosnian Croat war crimes suspects found on its territory.
Most of the suspects are thought to live in Bosnia, but the independent weekly Tjednik said on Friday at least two presently resided in Croatia.

Granic said officials from Croatia and Bosnia were now working on a joint declaration to pave the way for a meeting between Tudjman and chairman of Bosnia's collective presidency Alija Izetbegovic, but gave no details.

The meeting, intended to give a fresh impetus to the Federation, has been postponed several times. The apparent reason was Croatia's failure to rein in Bosnian Croats in Mostar, who opposed forming a joint police force in the southern Herzegovina region.

"When it comes to forming the joint police force in Bosnia, we admit to having certain influence on the political leadership in Herzegovina, but by no means can we be held reponsible for day-to-day local events there," Granic said.

On the issue of refugee return, he said the government would immediately start preparing the return of some 7,800 Serbs who opted to stay in Croatian and enable those wishing to leave to sell their property at fair terms.
"The return will be organised for all those who want it," he told reporters.
Last month U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright visited Croatia to publicly reprimand the government for tolerating harassment of elderly Serbs who tried to return to their original homes.
Some 120,000 Croatian Serbs now live under United Nations administration in their last enclave of Eastern Slavonia. About a half are refugees from elswhere in Croatia.
The enclave is to revert under full Zagreb rule in January.
